translation: Seize the day.
origin: Horace, Odes 1.11, advising a woman named Leuconoe to stop consulting astrologers about the future. The verb literally means to pluck, as you would pick ripe fruit.
today: Not a call to party, but to stop postponing: use what is in front of you now, since tomorrow is not guaranteed.
image: Lawrence Alma-Tadema - Spring - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, Spring, 1894

translation: Remember that you will die.
origin: A Christian and monastic motto of the Middle Ages, rooted in older Stoic practice. The story of a slave whispering it to a Roman general in triumph is a later embellishment.
today: A quick way to put small worries in proportion and decide what is actually worth your time.
image: StillLifeWithASkull.jpg
credit: Philippe de Champaigne, Vanitas, c. 1646

translation: Make haste slowly.
origin: Suetonius says it was a favourite saying of Emperor Augustus, who quoted it in Greek. Renaissance printers later used it with the emblem of a dolphin wrapped around an anchor.
today: Speed and care are not opposites: rushing usually costs more time than it saves.
image: An Audience at Agrippa's, by Lawrence Alma-Tadema.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, An Audience at Agrippa's, 1876

translation: I came, I saw, I conquered.
origin: Julius Caesar's summary of his five-day victory at Zela in 47 BC. Suetonius says the three words were carried on a placard in his triumph.
today: Shorthand for a quick, clean win, and the gold standard of the short status update.
image: Andrea Mantegna (1431-1506) - The Triumphs of Caesar, 9. Caesar on his Chariot - RCIN 403966 - Royal Collection.jpg
credit: Andrea Mantegna, The Triumphs of Caesar, c. 1484–92

translation: The die is cast.
origin: Caesar on crossing the Rubicon in 49 BC, starting a civil war. Suetonius gives it in Latin; Plutarch says he actually spoke it in Greek, quoting the playwright Menander.
today: Used when a decision can no longer be undone, so there is no point looking back.
image: Jean Fouquet - Caesar Crossing the Rubicon - WGA08034.jpg
commons_info: Jean Fouquet | second half of 15th centurydate QS:P571,+1450-00-00T00:00:00Z/7 | Public domain
credit: Jean Fouquet, Caesar Crossing the Rubicon, c. 1470

translation: In wine, truth.
origin: An ancient proverb with Greek roots; Pliny the Elder already remarks that people commonly credit wine with truth.
today: People say what they really think after a few glasses. Whether that is a virtue depends on what they think.
image: Bacchus by Caravaggio 1.jpg
commons_info: Caravaggio | Original:  circa 1598date QS:P571,+1598-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P1480,Q5727902;  This version:  1 August 2021, 10:32:59 | Public domain
credit: Caravaggio, Bacchus, c. 1596

translation: Skill takes long, life is short.
origin: The Latin form of the first of Hippocrates' Aphorisms, where the art in question is medicine. Seneca repeats it at the start of On the Shortness of Life.
today: Any real craft takes longer to master than you expect, so start now and be patient with yourself.
image: Hippocrate refusant les présents d'Artaxerxès (original).JPG
credit: Anne-Louis Girodet, Hippocrates Refusing the Gifts of Artaxerxes, 1792

translation: Time flies.
origin: Shortened from Virgil, Georgics 3: fugit inreparabile tempus, irreplaceable time is fleeing. It became a favourite inscription on clocks and sundials.
today: A reminder that the hours you lose do not come back, usually read on a clock you are late for.
image: The dance to the music of time c. 1640.jpg
credit: Nicolas Poussin, A Dance to the Music of Time, c. 1634–36

translation: A sound mind in a sound body.
origin: Juvenal, Satires 10, listing the few things worth praying for, along with courage and freedom from greed and anger.
today: Now a gym slogan, but Juvenal's point was humbler: ask for health and good sense, not wealth or fame.
image: Young Spartans National Gallery NG3860.jpg
credit: Edgar Degas, Young Spartans Exercising, c. 1860

translation: Bread and circuses.
origin: Juvenal, Satires 10: the Roman people, who once handed out power and legions, now anxiously want only free grain and chariot races.
today: Said of any politics that keeps people quiet with handouts and entertainment instead of answers.
image: Jean-Leon_Gerome_Pollice_Verso.jpg
credit: Jean-Léon Gérôme, Pollice Verso, 1872

translation: If you want peace, prepare for war.
origin: A modern condensed form of a line by the late Roman military writer Vegetius: whoever desires peace, let him prepare for war.
today: The logic of deterrence, and, its critics would add, of every arms race.
image: Giulio Romano - The Battle of the Milvian Bridge.jpg
credit: Giulio Romano (Raphael's workshop), The Battle of the Milvian Bridge, 1520–24

translation: The voice of the people is the voice of God.
origin: A medieval saying. Alcuin of York quoted it in a letter to Charlemagne in 798 only to warn against it, since the crowd's riots are close to madness.
today: Worth remembering both ways: majorities matter, and majorities can be wrong.
image: Raban-Maur Alcuin Otgar.jpg
credit: Hrabanus Maurus, presented by Alcuin, offers his book to Archbishop Otgar, manuscript, 9th century

translation: Let the buyer beware.
origin: A maxim of sales law, especially in English common law: the buyer must check the goods, and the seller need not point out every flaw.
today: Read the small print, test before you pay, and do not expect the seller to do your homework.
image: Sale of bread fresco from Pompeii restored.jpg
credit: Fresco of a bread stall, Pompeii, 1st century

translation: The law is harsh, but it is the law.
origin: A legal maxim distilled from a passage of the jurist Ulpian in Justinian's Digest, admitting a rule is very hard but is how the law is written.
today: Rules apply even when the outcome feels unfair. The fix is to change the rule, not to ignore it.
image: David Brutus.jpg
credit: Jacques-Louis David, The Lictors Bring to Brutus the Bodies of His Sons, 1789

translation: The wolf in the story.
origin: Used by Terence in the Adelphoe and by Cicero in his letters, for someone who turns up just as people are talking about him.
today: The Latin for speak of the devil.
image: Vaticana, Vat. lat. 3868 (2r).jpg
commons_info: Unknown authorUnknown author | 9th centurydate QS:P,+850-00-00T00:00:00Z/7 | Public domain
credit: Terence manuscript, Vatican Library (Vat. lat. 3868), 9th century

translation: I shall not wholly die.
origin: Horace, Odes 3.30, the proud final poem of his collection: his verses will outlast him.
today: The hope behind any work meant to last. Horace was right; we are still quoting him.
image: Raphael - The Parnassus.jpg
credit: Raphael, The Parnassus, 1509–11

translation: I hate and I love.
origin: The opening of Catullus 85, a two-line poem about his affair with Lesbia: he cannot explain how, he only feels it, and it tortures him.
today: Still the most precise description of a relationship you cannot leave.
image: Catullus-at-Lesbia's-large.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, Catullus at Lesbia's, 1865

translation: Who benefits?
origin: Cicero, defending Sextus Roscius in 80 BC, cites the stern judge Lucius Cassius, who always asked this in criminal cases.
today: To understand why something happened, follow the advantage. Useful in courtrooms and in reading the news.
image: Jean-Léon Gérôme - The Death of Caesar - Walters 37884.jpg
credit: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Death of Caesar, 1859–67

translation: Oh the times, oh the customs!
origin: Cicero, First Speech against Catiline, 63 BC, outraged that a known conspirator could sit calmly in the Senate.
today: The timeless complaint about how things are going to the dogs. Usually said with a sigh, now often with irony.
image: Cicero_Denounces_Catiline_in_the_Roman_Senate_by_Cesare_Maccari.png
credit: Cesare Maccari, Cicero Denounces Catiline, 1880s

translation: Experience is the best teacher.
origin: Cicero, Pro Rabirio Postumo, in a passage about a man learning from his practical dealings.
today: True, but the fees are paid in mistakes.
image: Diego Velázquez - The Forge of Vulcan - WGA24376.jpg
credit: Diego Velázquez, The Forge of Vulcan, 1630

translation: Man proposes, but God disposes.
origin: Thomas a Kempis, The Imitation of Christ, a 15th-century devotional book, echoing an idea from Proverbs 16.
today: Make your plans, but hold them loosely. Most of what happens next is not up to you.
image: Pieter Bruegel the Elder - Landscape with the Fall of Icarus - Brussels, Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium - Google Arts & Culture.jpg
commons_info: After Pieter Brueghel the Elder | from 1582 until 1625date QS:P,+1500-00-00T00:00:00Z/6,P580,+1582-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P582,+1625-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (attr.), Landscape with the Fall of Icarus, c. 1560

translation: Dripping water hollows the stone.
origin: Ovid, Letters from the Black Sea 4.10. The popular addition, not by force but by falling often, is a later medieval extension.
today: Small, steady effort beats one big push. Good news for habits, bad news for grudges.
image: Le pont du Gard - Hubert Robert - Musée du Louvre Peintures INV 7650.jpg
credit: Hubert Robert, The Pont du Gard, 1786

translation: Dare to know.
origin: Horace, Epistles 1.2, urging a young friend to start living wisely now. In 1784 Kant made it the motto of the Enlightenment.
today: Have the courage to think for yourself instead of borrowing conclusions.
image: Horace, Virgil and Varius at the house of Maecenas.jpg
credit: Charles-François Jalabert, Virgil, Horace and Varius at the House of Maecenas, 1846

translation: Fortune favours the bold.
origin: Virgil, Aeneid 10, spoken by Turnus as he leads his men into battle. He is later killed by Aeneas.
today: Boldness does pay off, sometimes. Turnus is the reminder that the proverb has survivors' bias.
image: Aeneas and Turnus.jpg
credit: Luca Giordano, Aeneas Defeats Turnus, c. 1688

latin: Homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto
pronunciation: HOH-moh soom, hoo-MAH-nee NEE-hil ah meh ah-lee-AY-noom POO-toh
translation: I am human; nothing human is alien to me.
origin: Terence, The Self-Tormentor, 163 BC. A neighbour uses it to justify being nosy about another man's affairs.
today: Born as an excuse for curiosity, it became the motto of humanism and empathy.
image: Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema, English (born Netherlands) - A Reading from Homer - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, A Reading from Homer, 1885

translation: Woe to the vanquished.
origin: Livy, book 5: after sacking Rome around 390 BC, the Gallic chief Brennus used false weights for the ransom, and when the Romans protested he threw his sword on the scale.
today: The winner sets the terms. Said whenever the stronger side stops pretending to be fair.
image: Paul_Jamin_-_Le_Brenn_et_sa_part_de_butin_1893.jpg
credit: Paul Jamin, Brennus and His Share of the Spoils, 1893

translation: The world wants to be deceived, so let it be deceived.
origin: Not ancient, though often credited to Petronius. The first half appears in the 16th-century writer Sebastian Franck; the second half is traditionally attributed to Cardinal Carlo Carafa.
today: A cynic's business plan: if people prefer the illusion, someone will sell it to them.
image: Georges de La Tour - Cheater with the Ace of Diamonds - WGA12334.jpg
credit: Georges de La Tour, The Cheat with the Ace of Diamonds, c. 1635

translation: Money does not stink.
origin: Suetonius tells how Emperor Vespasian taxed the urine collected from public toilets; when his son objected, he held a coin to his nose and asked if it smelled.
today: Used when someone takes money without asking where it came from.
image: Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema, RA, OM - The Triumph of Titus - The Flavians - Walters 3731.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, The Triumph of Titus: AD 71, 1885

translation: Who will guard the guards themselves?
origin: Juvenal, Satires 6, on the futility of setting guards over an unfaithful wife: the guards can be bribed too.
today: The core question of any system of oversight: who checks the people doing the checking?
image: Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema, RA, OM - A Roman Emperor (Claudius) - Walters 37165.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, A Roman Emperor: AD 41, 1871

translation: Man is a wolf to man.
origin: Plautus, The Comedy of Asses, around 200 BC: a man is a wolf to a man when he does not know what sort he is. Hobbes made it famous in the 17th century.
today: A bleak view of human nature, and in the original a narrower one: trust is earned, not assumed.
image: Peter Paul Rubens - Romulus and Remus - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Peter Paul Rubens, Romulus and Remus, c. 1615–16

translation: Deep calls to deep.
origin: The Vulgate, Psalm 41 (42 in modern numbering), a lament in which waves of trouble follow one another.
today: One mistake or misfortune tends to drag the next behind it. Fix the first before it multiplies.
image: Francis Danby - The Deluge - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Francis Danby, The Deluge, c. 1840

translation: Laughter abounds in the mouth of fools.
origin: A medieval proverb, echoing Ecclesiastes on the laughter of fools.
today: Aimed at whoever laughs loudest at what they understand least.
image: Jheronimus Bosch 011.jpg
credit: Hieronymus Bosch, The Ship of Fools, c. 1500

translation: Now is the time to drink.
origin: Horace, Odes 1.37, written to celebrate the defeat and death of Cleopatra in 30 BC.
today: The classical way to say: let us open the bottle, it is over.
image: Giambattista Tiepolo - The Banquet of Cleopatra - Google Art Project.jpg
commons_info: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo | from 1743 until 1744date QS:P571,+1743-00-00T00:00:00Z/8,P580,+1743-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P582,+1744-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, The Banquet of Cleopatra, 1743–44

translation: There is no arguing about tastes.
origin: A maxim of medieval and early modern scholastic origin, not found in classical authors.
today: A polite way to end a debate nobody will win.
image: Vertumnus årstidernas gud målad av Giuseppe Arcimboldo 1591 - Skoklosters slott - 91503.jpg
credit: Giuseppe Arcimboldo, Vertumnus, 1591

translation: So many evils could religion persuade men to commit.
origin: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things, book 1, after describing Agamemnon sacrificing his daughter Iphigenia to win a fair wind.
today: Quoted against fanaticism of every kind, religious or not.
image: Giovanni_Battista_Tiepolo_-_The_Sacrifice_of_Iphigenia_-_Villa_Valmarana.jpg
credit: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, The Sacrifice of Iphigenia, 1757

translation: Sometimes even good Homer nods off.
origin: Horace, Art of Poetry: he is irritated when great Homer slips, though he admits that in a long work some drowsiness is forgivable.
today: Even the best make mistakes. Judge the whole work, not its weakest page.
image: Rembrandt - Aristotle with a Bust of Homer - WGA19232.jpg
credit: Rembrandt, Aristotle with a Bust of Homer, 1653

translation: Had you kept quiet, you would have remained a philosopher.
origin: A medieval rewording of a story in Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy: a man boasting he is a philosopher answers an insult with anger, and gives himself away.
today: Sometimes the smartest thing to say is nothing.
image: Boethius initial consolation philosophy.jpg
credit: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, illuminated initial, medieval manuscript

translation: Nothing comes from nothing.
origin: The principle goes back to Greek philosophy and Lucretius, who writes that nothing can be created from nothing. The compact Latin formula is later.
today: First law of physics, and of budgets: results need inputs.
image: Michelangelo, Separation of Light from Darkness 02.jpg
credit: Michelangelo, The Separation of Light from Darkness, 1512

translation: Beware of the dog.
origin: Petronius' Satyricon describes a painted dog with these words at a rich man's door. A famous mosaic with the same words survives at Pompeii.
today: The oldest door sign in the world still in use.
image: Karl Brullov - The Last Day of Pompeii - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Karl Bryullov, The Last Day of Pompeii, 1830–33

translation: Divide and rule.
origin: Not found in any ancient author. It is an early modern maxim of statecraft, often attached to Louis XI of France or to readings of Machiavelli.
today: Keep your opponents busy fighting each other. Watch for it in offices as much as in empires.
image: Le Jugement de Salomon - 1649 - Nicolas Poussin - Louvre - INV 7277 ; MR 2316 (2).jpg
credit: Nicolas Poussin, The Judgement of Solomon, 1649

latin: Errare humanum est, perseverare autem diabolicum
pronunciation: er-RAH-reh hoo-MAH-noom est, per-seh-weh-RAH-reh OW-tem dee-ah-BOH-li-koom
translation: To err is human, but to persist is diabolical.
origin: The first half echoes Cicero and Seneca; the second half comes from Christian writing, close to a sermon of Saint Augustine.
today: Mistakes are forgivable. Repeating them after you have been warned is a choice.
image: Sandro Botticelli 052.jpg
credit: Sandro Botticelli, Saint Augustine in His Study, 1480

translation: Know yourself.
origin: The Latin form of gnothi seauton, carved at the temple of Apollo at Delphi and taken up by Socrates.
today: Most bad decisions start with a wrong idea of who we are and what we want.
image: John Collier - Priestess of Delphi - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: John Collier, Priestess of Delphi, 1891

translation: I think, therefore I am.
origin: René Descartes. He first wrote it in French in 1637; the Latin version appears in his Principles of Philosophy, 1644.
today: The one thing you cannot doubt is that you are doubting. Everything else needs evidence.
image: Frans Hals - Portret van René Descartes.jpg
credit: After Frans Hals, Portrait of René Descartes, c. 1649

translation: Nature does not make jumps.
origin: An early modern principle of natural philosophy, used by Leibniz and by the botanist Linnaeus in 1751; Darwin quotes it too.
today: Change usually happens by small steps, even when it looks sudden from far away.
image: Haeckel Actiniae.jpg
credit: Ernst Haeckel, Art Forms in Nature, 1904

translation: Love conquers all.
origin: Virgil, Eclogues 10, the last line of the collection, which goes on: and let us too yield to love.
today: Usually quoted as a happy ending. In Virgil it is a surrender.
image: Caravaggio - Cupid as Victor - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Caravaggio, Amor Vincit Omnia, 1602

translation: Relentless work conquered everything.
origin: Virgil, Georgics 1, explaining how humans had to invent farming once Jupiter made life hard. The word improbus means relentless, even wicked.
today: Often trimmed to labor omnia vincit and used as a motto of hard work. Virgil meant it with a sigh.
image: Jean Baptiste Joseph Wicar - Virgil Reading the "Aeneid" to Augustus, Octavia, and Livia - 1963.258 - Art Institute of Chicago.jpg
credit: Jean-Baptiste Wicar, Virgil Reading the Aeneid to Augustus, Octavia and Livia, 1790

translation: I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts.
origin: Virgil, Aeneid 2, said by the priest Laocoon as the Trojans debate whether to bring the wooden horse inside the walls.
today: Be wary of generosity from people who have every reason to harm you.
image: The_Procession_of_the_Trojan_Horse_in_Troy_by_Giovanni_Domenico_Tiepolo_(cropped).jpg
credit: Giovanni Domenico Tiepolo, The Procession of the Trojan Horse into Troy, c. 1760

translation: Thus passes the glory of the world.
origin: Spoken at papal coronations from the 15th century, while a bundle of flax was burned before the new pope. It echoes The Imitation of Christ.
today: Success fades fast. Enjoy it, and do not mistake it for something permanent.
image: Cole_Thomas_The_Course_of_Empire_Desolation_1836.jpg
credit: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: Desolation, 1836

translation: You too, Brutus?
origin: Not in any ancient source. Suetonius reports that Caesar may have said, in Greek, you too, child? The Latin line was made famous by Shakespeare.
today: The cry of anyone betrayed by someone they trusted.
image: Vincenzo Camuccini, The Death of Julius Caesar (detail).jpg
credit: Vincenzo Camuccini, The Death of Julius Caesar (detail), 1804–05

translation: The play is over.
origin: Traditionally the last words of Augustus. Suetonius actually reports him asking, in Greek verse, whether he had played his part well, and asking for applause.
today: Said when something has reached its end and there is nothing more to add.
image: Lawrence Alma-Tadema - The Entrance to a Roman Theatre (1866) - painting.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, Entrance to a Roman Theatre, 1866

translation: What an artist dies in me.
origin: Suetonius, Life of Nero: the emperor's repeated lament as he prepared his own suicide in AD 68.
today: For anyone whose self-image survives every evidence to the contrary.
image: Vasiliy_smirnov_001.jpg
credit: Vasily Smirnov, The Death of Nero, 1888

translation: Hannibal is at the gates.
origin: After Cannae in 216 BC, Romans feared Hannibal would march on the city. Cicero and Livy use the phrase for a danger close at hand.
today: Said when a threat is no longer theoretical and it is time to act.
image: Joseph Mallord William Turner - Snow Storm, Hannibal and his Army Crossing the Alps - WGA23167.jpg
commons_info: J. M. W. Turner | 1812date QS:P571,+1812-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: J. M. W. Turner, Snow Storm: Hannibal and His Army Crossing the Alps, 1812

translation: Carthage must be destroyed.
origin: Cato the Elder reportedly ended every speech in the Senate with this demand, whatever the subject. Plutarch tells it in Greek; the Latin formula is later.
today: The power, and the obsessiveness, of repeating one point until it wins.
image: Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - The Decline of the Carthaginian Empire ... - N00499 - National Gallery.jpg
commons_info: J. M. W. Turner | 1817 | Public domain
credit: J. M. W. Turner, The Decline of the Carthaginian Empire, 1817

translation: Without anger or bias.
origin: Tacitus, at the start of the Annals, promising to write the history of the emperors without hatred or partisanship.
today: The ideal of fair reporting, and a useful test for anything you are about to post.
image: Nicolas Poussin - The Death of Germanicus - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Nicolas Poussin, The Death of Germanicus, 1627

translation: They make a desert and call it peace.
origin: Tacitus, Agricola 30, in a speech he gives to the Caledonian chief Calgacus against Roman conquest.
today: Said when the word peace is used to cover destruction.
image: Cole Thomas The Course of Empire Destruction 1836.jpg
credit: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: Destruction, 1836

translation: Everything unknown is taken as grand.
origin: Tacitus, Agricola 30, in the same speech of Calgacus: the Romans seem more fearsome because they are far away and unknown.
today: Distance and mystery inflate reputations. Things look smaller up close.
image: William Bell Scott (1811-1890) - The Romans Cause a Wall to Be Built for the Protection of the South - 584365 - National Trust.jpg
credit: William Bell Scott, Building the Roman Wall, 1857

translation: When the state is most corrupt, the laws are most numerous.
origin: Tacitus, Annals 3.27, in a digression on how Roman law multiplied as public life decayed.
today: A flood of new rules is often a symptom, not a cure.
image: Thomas Couture - Romans during the Decadence - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Thomas Couture, Romans of the Decadence, 1847

latin: Optimum est pati quod emendare non possis
pronunciation: OP-ti-moom est PAH-tee kwod eh-men-DAH-reh nohn POS-sis
translation: It is best to endure what you cannot change.
origin: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 107, a classic statement of Stoic acceptance.
today: Spend your energy on what you can fix, and stop fighting the weather.
image: David - The Death of Socrates.jpg
credit: Jacques-Louis David, The Death of Socrates, 1787

translation: We learn not for life, but for school.
origin: Seneca, Letters 106, complaining about philosophy taught as clever puzzles. Teachers later flipped it into the motto non scholae sed vitae.
today: The original is the more honest version. Ask whether what you study will survive the exam.
image: Jan Steen - The Village School (National Gallery of Ireland).jpg
credit: Jan Steen, The Village School, c. 1665

translation: All that is mine I carry with me.
origin: Attributed to the Greek sage Bias of Priene as he fled his city without luggage; Cicero quotes it in Latin in the Paradoxa Stoicorum.
today: What truly belongs to you is what you know and who you are, not what you own.
image: Jean-Léon Gérôme - Diogenes - Walters 37131.jpg
credit: Jean-Léon Gérôme, Diogenes, 1860

translation: Leisure with dignity.
origin: Cicero, Pro Sestio, describing the goal of good citizens: peace and honour, rest earned after public service.
today: The ideal retirement, or a well-earned weekend.
image: Under the Roof of Blue Ionian Weather, Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, Under the Roof of Blue Ionian Weather, 1901

translation: History is the teacher of life.
origin: Cicero, On the Orator, book 2, in a list of praises of history.
today: History teaches, the joke goes, but has very few students.
image: Jan Vermeer - The Art of Painting - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Johannes Vermeer, The Art of Painting, c. 1666–68

translation: The strictest law is the greatest injustice.
origin: Cicero, On Duties 1.33, quoting it as an already well-worn proverb.
today: Applying rules to the letter, without judgement, can produce the very wrong they were meant to prevent.
image: Delacroix - The Justice of Trajan, oil on canvas, 1858.jpg
credit: Eugène Delacroix, The Justice of Trajan, 1858

translation: For laws fall silent amid arms.
origin: Cicero, Pro Milone 11, arguing that killing in self-defence can be lawful.
today: In war and emergencies, rights are the first casualties. A warning, not a permission.
image: John Vanderlyn - Caius Marius Amid the Ruins of Carthage - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: John Vanderlyn, Caius Marius amid the Ruins of Carthage, 1807

translation: Let the welfare of the people be the supreme law.
origin: Cicero, On the Laws 3.8, in his model constitution for a republic. It is the motto of the state of Missouri.
today: A noble principle, and one that has justified both great reforms and great abuses.
image: Jacques-Louis David - Oath of the Horatii - Google Art Project.jpg
commons_info: Anne-Louis Girodet / After Jacques-Louis David | 1786 (original by David made in 1784) | Public domain
credit: Jacques-Louis David and Anne-Louis Girodet, Oath of the Horatii, 1786

translation: How much longer, then?
origin: The opening of Cicero's First Speech against Catiline, 63 BC: how long will you abuse our patience, Catiline?
today: The two words to quote when your patience has run out.
image: Appio Claudio Cieco in Senato.jpg
credit: Cesare Maccari, Appius Claudius Caecus in the Senate, 1880s

translation: Agreements must be kept.
origin: A principle of canon law and later of international law, set out by Hugo Grotius in the 17th century.
today: The foundation of every contract and treaty: a promise is binding.
image: Westfaelischer Friede in Muenster (Gerard Terborch 1648).jpg
credit: Gerard ter Borch, The Ratification of the Treaty of Münster, 1648

translation: No one should be judge in their own case.
origin: A principle of Roman law, found in Justinian's Code, and a pillar of natural justice ever since.
today: The reason conflicts of interest matter, from courts to performance reviews.
image: Rubens - Judgement of Paris.jpg
credit: Peter Paul Rubens, The Judgement of Paris, c. 1636

translation: Let the other side be heard too.
origin: A principle of Roman and medieval law. Seneca's Medea already says that a judge who rules without hearing both sides is unjust, even if his verdict is right.
today: Before you take sides, ask for the other version of the story.
image: Sandro Botticelli La calumnia de Apeles.jpg
credit: Sandro Botticelli, The Calumny of Apelles, c. 1494–95

translation: Who stays silent seems to consent.
origin: One of the rules of law in the canon law collection of Pope Boniface VIII, 1298. It continues: when he ought and could have spoken.
today: Silence is often read as agreement. If you disagree, say so.
image: Bonifacius VIII - Fresco in Lateran.jpg
credit: Giotto (attr.), Boniface VIII Proclaims the Jubilee, 1300

translation: He gives twice who gives quickly.
origin: A short form of a line by Publilius Syrus, a former slave whose one-line maxims Romans learned at school: to the poor, quick help is a double gift.
today: Help that arrives on time is worth twice as much as help that arrives late.
image: El Greco - San Martín y el mendigo.jpg
credit: El Greco, Saint Martin and the Beggar, 1597–99

latin: Fortuna vitrea est: tum cum splendet frangitur
pronunciation: for-TOO-nah WI-treh-ah est: toom koom SPLEN-det FRAHN-gi-toor
translation: Fortune is made of glass: just when it shines, it breaks.
origin: Publilius Syrus, Sentences, 1st century BC.
today: The moment of greatest success is also the most fragile one.
image: Dosso Dossi (Giovanni di Niccolò de Lutero) (Italian (Ferrarese) - Allegory of Fortune - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Dosso Dossi, Allegory of Fortune, c. 1530

translation: Labours are pleasant once completed.
origin: Cicero, On Ends 2.105, quoting it as a proverb.
today: The hard project always looks better in the rear-view mirror.
credit: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: The Arcadian or Pastoral State, 1834

translation: Let arms yield to the toga.
origin: A line from Cicero's own poem on his consulship, quoted in On Duties 1.77. The toga stands for civilian government.
today: Civilian authority must stand above the military.
image: Cincinato abandona el arado para dictar leyes a Roma, c.1806 de Juan Antonio Ribera.jpg
commons_info: Juan Antonio de Ribera | circa 1806date QS:P571,+1806-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P1480,Q5727902 | Public domain
credit: Juan Antonio Ribera, Cincinnatus Leaves the Plough, 1806

translation: I give so that you give.
origin: A Roman legal formula for exchange contracts, also used to describe Roman religion as a bargain with the gods.
today: Most favours come with an invoice, stated or not.
image: Titian - The Tribute Money - Google Art Project (715452).jpg
credit: Titian, The Tribute Money, c. 1516

latin: Oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente
pronunciation: OH-koo-loom proh OH-koo-loh, DEN-tem proh DEN-teh
translation: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.
origin: The Vulgate, Exodus 21:24, from the ancient law of retaliation, which originally capped revenge at an equal harm.
today: Meant as a limit on vengeance, often quoted as a licence for it.
image: Rembrandt - Moses with the Ten Commandments - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Rembrandt, Moses with the Ten Commandments, 1659

translation: Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
origin: The Vulgate, Ecclesiastes 1:2. Vanitas means emptiness, a breath of air.
today: A reminder that status, possessions and applause weigh less than they seem.
image: Harmen Steenwijck - Vanitas Still-Life - WGA21768.jpg
credit: Harmen Steenwyck, An Allegory of the Vanities of Human Life, c. 1640

translation: Nothing new under the sun.
origin: The Vulgate, Ecclesiastes 1:9.
today: Most hot takes, scandals and startups have a precedent. Look it up before you panic.
image: Pieter Bruegel the Elder - The Tower of Babel (Vienna) - Google Art Project - edited.jpg
commons_info: Pieter Bruegel the Elder | 1563date QS:P571,+1563-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Tower of Babel, 1563

translation: Physician, heal yourself.
origin: The Vulgate, Luke 4:23, a proverb Jesus expects his hometown to throw at him.
today: Before you advise others, fix the same problem in your own house.
image: Rembrandt van Rijn - The Hundred Guilder Print - 1942.757 - Cleveland Museum of Art.tif
credit: Rembrandt, Christ Healing the Sick (The Hundred Guilder Print), c. 1649

translation: Where are you going?
origin: From the Vulgate, John 13:36, and above all the apocryphal Acts of Peter: fleeing Rome, Peter meets Christ and asks Domine, quo vadis? He turns back to face martyrdom.
today: A question worth asking of any plan, career or company.
image: Domine,_quo_vadis.jpg
credit: Annibale Carracci, Domine, Quo Vadis?, 1601–02

latin: Pulvis es et in pulverem reverteris
pronunciation: POOL-wis es et in POOL-weh-rem reh-WER-teh-ris
translation: You are dust, and to dust you shall return.
origin: The Vulgate, Genesis 3:19, God to Adam after the Fall. Repeated every Ash Wednesday.
today: The original memento mori, two thousand years older.
image: Masaccio-TheExpulsionOfAdamAndEveFromEden-Restoration.jpg
commons_info: Masaccio | 1426-1428 (altered in 1680, and restored in 1980) | Public domain
credit: Masaccio, The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden, c. 1425

latin: Omnes qui acceperint gladium, gladio peribunt
pronunciation: OM-nays kwee ahk-KEH-peh-rint GLAH-dee-oom, GLAH-dee-oh peh-REE-boont
translation: All who take the sword will perish by the sword.
origin: The Vulgate, Matthew 26:52, Jesus to Peter after Peter cuts off a servant's ear at the arrest in Gethsemane.
today: Violence tends to come back to the one who starts it.
image: Giotto di Bondone - No. 31 Scenes from the Life of Christ - 15. The Arrest of Christ (Kiss of Judas) - WGA09216.jpg
credit: Giotto, The Kiss of Judas, c. 1305

latin: Spiritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma
pronunciation: SPEE-ri-toos KWI-dem PROMP-toos est, KAH-roh OW-tem in-FIR-mah
translation: The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.
origin: The Vulgate, Matthew 26:41, Jesus finding his disciples asleep in Gethsemane.
today: Good intentions, meet the second slice of cake.
image: Mantegna, Andrea - Agony in the Garden - National Gallery, London.jpg
credit: Andrea Mantegna, The Agony in the Garden, c. 1458–60

latin: Nemo propheta acceptus est in patria sua
pronunciation: NEH-moh proh-FAY-tah ahk-KEP-toos est in PAH-tree-ah SOO-ah
translation: No prophet is accepted in his own country.
origin: The Vulgate, Luke 4:24, Jesus on being rejected in Nazareth.
today: The people who knew you before are often the last to take you seriously.
image: John Everett Millais - Christ in the House of His Parents (`The Carpenter's Shop') - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: John Everett Millais, Christ in the House of His Parents, 1849–50

translation: The mouth speaks from the fullness of the heart.
origin: The Vulgate, Matthew 12:34.
today: What people talk about most tells you what they care about most.
image: Bloch-SermonOnTheMount.jpg
credit: Carl Bloch, The Sermon on the Mount, 1877

translation: The fox changes its fur, not its habits.
origin: Suetonius, Life of Vespasian, where a herdsman throws the proverb at the emperor over his greed.
today: People can change their look much faster than their character.
image: Reineke Fuchs - Kaulbach (150110108).jpg
credit: Wilhelm von Kaulbach, illustration for Reynard the Fox, 1846

translation: The donkey rubs the donkey.
origin: A medieval proverb about donkeys scratching each other's backs.
today: Said of mediocre people who flatter each other in public.
image: Museo del Prado - Goya - Caprichos - No. 39 - Asta su Abuelo.jpg
credit: Francisco Goya, Los Caprichos: As Far Back as His Grandfather, 1799

translation: One hand washes the other.
origin: Used by Petronius in the Satyricon and by Seneca in his satire on the emperor Claudius; it translates an older Greek proverb.
today: Favours are exchanged. Sometimes that is teamwork, sometimes it is corruption.
image: Roberto Bompiani - A Roman Feast - 72.PA.4 - J. Paul Getty Museum.jpg
commons_info: Roberto Bompiani | late 19th centurydate QS:P571,+1850-00-00T00:00:00Z/7,P4241,Q40719766 | Public domain
credit: Roberto Bompiani, A Roman Feast, late 19th century

translation: The eagle does not catch flies.
origin: A medieval and Renaissance proverb.
today: Do not waste your energy on petty quarrels beneath your level.
image: Studio of Melchior de Hondecoeter An Eagle, a Cockerell, Hens, a Pigeon In Flight and Other Birds.jpg
commons_info: Workshop of Melchior d'Hondecoeter | 17th centurydate QS:P571,+1650-00-00T00:00:00Z/7 | Public domain
credit: Studio of Melchior d'Hondecoeter, An Eagle with Other Birds, 17th century

translation: On the Greek Kalends.
origin: Suetonius says Augustus used it for debts that would never be paid: the Kalends were Roman, and the Greek calendar had none.
today: The Latin for when pigs fly.
image: Les Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry Janvier.jpg
credit: Limbourg brothers, Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry: January, c. 1412–16

translation: Shoemaker, not above the sandal.
origin: Pliny the Elder: a shoemaker correctly criticised a sandal in a painting by Apelles, then started criticising the leg, and the painter put him in his place.
today: Stick to what you know before you correct the experts.
image: Willem van Haecht - Alexander the Great visits the studio of Apelles N08610-169-lr-1.jpg
credit: Willem van Haecht, The Studio of Apelles, c. 1630

translation: No day without a line.
origin: Pliny the Elder says the painter Apelles never let a day pass without drawing at least one line. The phrase itself was coined later, from his account.
today: Small daily practice beats occasional bursts of inspiration.
image: Tiepolo - Apelles Painting the Portrait of Campaspe, About 1726, 1945.929.jpg
commons_info: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo | circa 1726date QS:P571,+1726-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P1480,Q5727902 | Public domain
credit: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, Apelles Painting Campaspe, c. 1725–26

translation: Further beyond.
origin: Motto of Emperor Charles V from 1516, defying the old warning that nothing lay beyond the Pillars of Hercules. It is still on the coat of arms of Spain.
today: Do not accept the edge of the map as the edge of the world.
image: Carlos V en Mühlberg, by Titian, from Prado in Google Earth.jpg
credit: Titian, Charles V at Mühlberg, 1548

latin: Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori
pronunciation: DOOL-keh et deh-KOH-room est proh PAH-tree-ah MOH-ree
translation: It is sweet and fitting to die for one's country.
origin: Horace, Odes 3.2. In 1917 the soldier-poet Wilfred Owen called it the old lie, in his poem about a gas attack.
today: Quoted today as often in Owen's bitter sense as in Horace's.

translation: The golden mean.
origin: Horace, Odes 2.10: whoever loves the golden mean avoids both a squalid hovel and an envied palace.
today: Not mediocrity, but balance: enough, without excess.
image: Richard Wilson - Distant View of Maecenas' Villa, Tivoli - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Richard Wilson, Distant View of Maecenas' Villa, Tivoli, 1756–57

translation: Be astonished by nothing.
origin: Horace, Epistles 1.6, presenting calm detachment as the key to a happy life.
today: The Stoic version of keep calm, and the cynic's excuse for never being impressed.
image: Diego Velázquez 022.jpg
credit: Diego Velázquez, Menippus, c. 1638

translation: The mountains will be in labour, and a ridiculous mouse will be born.
origin: Horace, Art of Poetry, mocking poets who promise epic grandeur and deliver very little.
today: For any huge announcement that ends in a tiny result.
image: Joseph Wright of Derby - Vesuvius in Eruption, with a View over the Islands in the Bay of Naples - Google Art Project.jpg
commons_info: Joseph Wright of Derby | circa 1776date QS:P571,+1776-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P1480,Q5727902 | Public domain
credit: Joseph Wright of Derby, Vesuvius in Eruption, c. 1776–80

translation: Anger is a brief madness.
origin: Horace, Epistles 1.2, advising his young friend to rule his temper before it rules him.
today: Do not send the email while you are angry.
image: Jacques-Louis David - The Anger of Achilles - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Jacques-Louis David, The Anger of Achilles, 1819

latin: Naturam expelles furca, tamen usque recurret
pronunciation: nah-TOO-rahm eks-PEL-lays FOOR-kah, TAH-men OOS-kweh reh-KOOR-ret
translation: Drive out nature with a pitchfork, it will still come back.
origin: Horace, Epistles 1.10, praising country life over the city.
today: Character and habits return, however hard you push them away.
image: Giovanni Paolo Panini (1691-1765) - Capriccio of Roman Ruins with the Colosseum - PD.107-1992 - Fitzwilliam Museum.jpg
credit: Giovanni Paolo Panini, Capriccio of Roman Ruins, 1737

latin: Caelum, non animum, mutant qui trans mare currunt
pronunciation: KY-loom, nohn AH-ni-moom, MOO-tahnt kwee trahns MAH-reh KOOR-roont
translation: Those who rush across the sea change their sky, not their soul.
origin: Horace, Epistles 1.11, to a restless friend touring the Greek islands.
today: Travel changes the scenery. Your problems fly with you.
image: Joseph Mallord William Turner - Ancient Rome; Agrippina Landing with the Ashes of Germanicus - Google Art Project.jpg
commons_info: J. M. W. Turner | 1837 | Public domain
credit: J. M. W. Turner, Ancient Rome: Agrippina Landing with the Ashes of Germanicus, 1839

translation: There is a measure in things.
origin: Horace, Satires 1.1: there are fixed limits, beyond and short of which what is right cannot stand.
today: Most virtues turn into vices when pushed too far.
image: Giotto. Allegorieën van de deugden en ondeugden Temperantia en ira (woede), GD015961.jpg
credit: Giotto, Temperance, c. 1305

translation: We are dust and shadow.
origin: Horace, Odes 4.7, a spring poem that turns into a meditation on death.
today: Perspective in four words.
image: Arnold Boecklin - Island of the Dead, Third Version.JPG
credit: Arnold Böcklin, Isle of the Dead, 1883

latin: Eheu fugaces, Postume, Postume, labuntur anni
pronunciation: EH-heh-oo foo-GAH-kays, POS-too-meh, POS-too-meh, lah-BOON-toor AHN-nee
translation: Alas, Postumus, Postumus, the fleeting years slip by.
origin: The opening of Horace, Odes 2.14, addressed to a friend who cannot stop time with any amount of piety.
today: The feeling you get on every birthday after thirty.
image: Nicolas Poussin - Et in Arcadia ego (deuxième version).jpg
credit: Nicolas Poussin, Et in Arcadia Ego, c. 1637–38

translation: There are tears in things.
origin: Virgil, Aeneid 1: Aeneas, in Carthage, sees the Trojan War painted on a temple wall and weeps.
today: The world itself has a sadness, and great art lets us feel it.
image: Énée et Didon, Guérin.jpg
commons_info: Pierre-Narcisse Guérin | circa 1815date QS:P571,+1815-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P1480,Q5727902, photo: 2024-01-29 08:23:52 | Public domain
credit: Pierre-Narcisse Guérin, Aeneas Tells Dido the Misfortunes of Troy, 1815

latin: Forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit
pronunciation: FOR-sahn et hyk OH-lim meh-mi-NIS-seh yoo-WAH-bit
translation: Perhaps one day it will be pleasing to remember even this.
origin: Virgil, Aeneid 1, Aeneas comforting his shipwrecked companions.
today: Today's disaster may be tomorrow's best story.
image: Aeneas' Flight from Troy by Federico Barocci.jpg
credit: Federico Barocci, Aeneas' Flight from Troy, 1598

translation: The descent to the underworld is easy.
origin: Virgil, Aeneid 6, the Sibyl warning Aeneas: going down is easy, coming back up is the real work.
today: Getting into trouble takes a moment. Getting out takes effort.
image: Joseph Mallord William Turner - Lake Avernus- Aeneas and the Cumaean Sybil - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: J. M. W. Turner, Lake Avernus: Aeneas and the Cumaean Sibyl, 1814–15

latin: Felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas
pronunciation: FAY-liks kwee POH-too-it RAY-room kog-NOS-keh-reh KOW-sahs
translation: Happy is he who could learn the causes of things.
origin: Virgil, Georgics 2, often read as a tribute to Lucretius and his scientific view of the world.
today: Understanding why things happen is one of the quieter forms of happiness.
image: Augustins - Eruption du Vesuve - Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes 78 1 1.jpg
commons_info: Didier Descouens | Taken on 16 February 2018 | Public domain
credit: Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes, The Eruption of Vesuvius, 24 August AD 79, 1813

translation: The accursed hunger for gold.
origin: Virgil, Aeneid 3, after the story of a Trojan prince murdered for his treasure: to what do you not drive mortal hearts?
today: Sacra here means accursed. Greed has not changed its methods.
image: Midas Washing at the Source of the Pactolus MET DP123854.jpg
credit: Nicolas Poussin, Midas Washing at the Source of the Pactolus, c. 1627

translation: I see the better and approve it; I follow the worse.
origin: Ovid, Metamorphoses 7, Medea torn between duty and her passion for Jason.
today: The classic description of knowing what is right and doing the opposite.
image: Eugène Delacroix - Medea about to Kill her Children - Musée du Louvre.jpg
credit: Eugène Delacroix, Medea About to Kill Her Children, 1862

translation: Time, devourer of things.
origin: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15, in the speech of Pythagoras on how everything changes.
today: Nothing escapes time. Build things that age well.
image: Pompeo Girolamo Batoni - Time orders Old Age to destroy Beauty.jpg
credit: Pompeo Batoni, Time Orders Old Age to Destroy Beauty, 1746

translation: Resist the beginnings.
origin: Ovid, Remedies for Love: stop a passion at the start, before it grows too strong to cure.
today: Habits, debts and bad ideas are easiest to stop on day one.
image: The Love of Paris and Helen by Jacques-Louis David.jpg
credit: Jacques-Louis David, The Loves of Paris and Helen, 1788

latin: Donec eris felix, multos numerabis amicos
pronunciation: DOH-nek EH-ris FAY-liks, MOOL-tohs noo-meh-RAH-bis ah-MEE-kohs
translation: As long as you are lucky, you will count many friends.
origin: Ovid, Sorrows (Tristia) 1.9, written in exile, when most friends had disappeared.
today: You learn who your friends are when things go badly.
image: Eugène Delacroix - Ovide chez les Scythes (1862).jpg
credit: Eugène Delacroix, Ovid among the Scythians, 1862

translation: He who has hidden well has lived well.
origin: Ovid, Sorrows (Tristia) 3.4, from exile, after his fame had ruined him. It echoes the Greek advice of Epicurus to live unnoticed.
today: A case for a quiet life in a loud age.
image: Turner Ovid Banished from Rome.jpg
commons_info: J. M. W. Turner | 1838date QS:P571,+1838-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: J. M. W. Turner, Ovid Banished from Rome, 1838

latin: Res est solliciti plena timoris amor
pronunciation: rays est sol-LI-ki-tee PLAY-nah ti-MOH-ris AH-mor
translation: Love is a thing full of anxious fear.
origin: Ovid, Heroines 1, Penelope writing to the absent Ulysses.
today: Anyone who has waited for a reply knows.
image: JohnWilliamWaterhouse-PenelopeandtheSuitors(1912).jpg
commons_info: John William Waterhouse | 1912date QS:P571,+1912-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: John William Waterhouse, Penelope and the Suitors, 1912

translation: The anger of kings is always heavy.
origin: Seneca, Medea, in a warning about provoking the powerful.
today: The bigger the boss, the more expensive the tantrum.
image: Rembrandt-Belsazar.jpg
credit: Rembrandt, Belshazzar's Feast, c. 1635–38

translation: Through hardship to the stars.
origin: A later motto, not a classical quotation. The idea comes from Seneca's Hercules Furens: there is no easy way from the earth to the stars.
today: Anything high is reached the hard way.
image: Annibale Carracci, Hercules at the Crossroads, brighter.jpg
credit: Annibale Carracci, Hercules at the Crossroads, c. 1596

latin: Omnia aliena sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est
pronunciation: OM-nee-ah ah-lee-AY-nah soont, TEM-poos TAN-toom NOS-troom est
translation: Everything else belongs to others; only time is ours.
origin: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 1, the opening letter of the collection.
today: Guard your time more carefully than your money.
image: Peter Paul Rubens - Dying Seneca.jpg
credit: Peter Paul Rubens, The Dying Seneca, c. 1612–13

translation: While we postpone, life speeds by.
origin: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 1.
today: The plan to start living later is the most common plan of all.
image: The Roses of Heliogabalus.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, The Roses of Heliogabalus, 1888

translation: By teaching, we learn.
origin: Condensed from Seneca, Letters 7: people learn while they teach.
today: Explain something to someone else and you will discover how well you know it.
image: "The School of Athens" by Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino.jpg
credit: Raphael, The School of Athens, 1509–11

latin: Quod sis esse velis nihilque malis
pronunciation: kwod sees ES-seh WEH-lis nee-HIL-kweh MAH-lees
translation: Want to be what you are, and prefer nothing else.
origin: Martial, Epigrams 10.47, a recipe for the happy life.
today: Contentment is not having everything. It is not wanting to be someone else.
image: Alma-Tadema Unconscious Rivals 1893.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, Unconscious Rivals, 1893

latin: Non est vivere, sed valere vita est
pronunciation: nohn est WEE-weh-reh, sed wah-LAY-reh WEE-tah est
translation: Life is not just living, but being well.
origin: Martial, Epigrams 6.70.
today: A long life is worth little without health to enjoy it.
image: The Baths at Caracalla.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, The Baths of Caracalla, 1899

latin: Sera nimis vita est crastina: vive hodie
pronunciation: SEH-rah NI-mis WEE-tah est KRAHS-ti-nah: WEE-weh HOH-dee-eh
translation: Tomorrow's life is too late: live today.
origin: Martial, Epigrams 1.15, to a friend who keeps postponing enjoyment.
today: Martial's sharper version of carpe diem.
image: Lawrence Alma-Tadema - The vintage festival - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, The Vintage Festival, 1871

translation: Honesty is praised, and left out in the cold.
origin: Juvenal, Satires 1, on a Rome where vice gets rich.
today: Everyone applauds integrity. Few pay for it.
image: Belisaire demandant l'aumone Jacques-Louis David.jpg
credit: Jacques-Louis David, Belisarius Begging for Alms, 1781

translation: A rare bird.
origin: Juvenal, Satires 6: a perfect wife is a rare bird on earth, as rare as a black swan.
today: Something or someone truly exceptional. Black swans, it turned out, exist.
image: Fabritius-vink.jpg
credit: Carel Fabritius, The Goldfinch, 1654

translation: The greatest respect is owed to a child.
origin: Juvenal, Satires 14, warning parents that children copy their vices.
today: Kids learn more from what you do than from what you say.
image: Jan Steen - 'As the Old Sing, So Pipe the Young' - 742 - Mauritshuis.jpg
credit: Jan Steen, As the Old Sing, So Pipe the Young, c. 1665

translation: Indignation makes the verse.
origin: Juvenal, Satires 1: even without talent, outrage at Rome's corruption makes him write poetry.
today: Anger is a powerful engine for writing, and for social media.
image: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes - The sleep of reason produces monsters (No. 43), from Los Caprichos - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Francisco Goya, The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters, 1799

translation: The traveller with empty pockets will sing in front of the robber.
origin: Juvenal, Satires 10, on how wealth brings fear.
today: The less you have, the less you have to lose.
image: Pieter Bruegel d. Ä. 035.jpg
commons_info: Pieter Bruegel the Elder | 1568 | Public domain
credit: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Misanthrope, 1568

translation: It is hard not to write satire.
origin: Juvenal, Satires 1, looking at the absurdities of Rome.
today: Some days the news writes the jokes for you.
image: Henryk Siemiradzki 004.jpeg
credit: Henryk Siemiradzki, Roman Orgy in the Time of the Caesars, 1872

translation: No one became utterly vile all at once.
origin: Juvenal, Satires 2.
today: Moral decline happens in small steps. Watch the small ones.
image: RemorsodeNero.jpg
commons_info: John William Waterhouse | 1878date QS:P571,+1878-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: John William Waterhouse, The Remorse of Nero, 1878

translation: As many people, so many opinions.
origin: Terence, Phormio, in a comic scene where three advisers give three different answers.
today: Ask a committee and you will get one opinion per member.
image: Pieter Brueghel the Elder - The Dutch Proverbs - Google Art Project.jpg
commons_info: Pieter Bruegel the Elder | 1559 | Public domain
credit: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, Netherlandish Proverbs, 1559

latin: Nullum est iam dictum quod non sit dictum prius
pronunciation: NOOL-loom est yahm DIK-toom kwod nohn sit DIK-toom PREE-oos
translation: Nothing is said now that has not been said before.
origin: Terence, prologue to The Eunuch, defending himself against charges of copying.
today: Originality is rare. Good execution is what counts.
image: Lawrence Alma-Tadema A Roman Art Lover 1.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, A Roman Art Lover, 1868

translation: A word to the wise is enough.
origin: Plautus, The Persian, and Terence, Phormio; abbreviated as verbum sap.
today: Clever people do not need everything spelled out.
image: Dürer - Käuzchen, Albertina 3123.jpg
credit: Albrecht Dürer, Little Owl, 1508

translation: The name is a sign.
origin: Derived from Plautus, The Persian, where a character's name, Lucris, is taken as a good omen of profit.
today: Names shape expectations. Choose them carefully, for products and children.
image: William Blake (1757-1827) - Adam Naming the Beasts - PC.95 - Pollok House.jpg
credit: William Blake, Adam Naming the Beasts, 1810

translation: I have wasted my oil and my effort.
origin: Plautus, The Little Carthaginian; the oil is lamp oil burned while working late.
today: For hours of work that came to nothing.
image: Joseph Wright of Derby The Alchemist.jpg
commons_info: Joseph Wright of Derby | 1771date QS:P571,+1771-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: Joseph Wright of Derby, The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, 1771

translation: Death is certain, its hour uncertain.
origin: A medieval proverb, often written on sundials and church clocks.
today: Since you do not know when, do not leave the important things for later.
image: The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg
commons_info: Pieter Bruegel the Elder | circa 1562date QS:P571,+1562-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P1480,Q5727902 | Public domain
credit: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Triumph of Death, c. 1562

translation: Spoken words fly away, written ones remain.
origin: A medieval proverb, sometimes linked to a speech by a Roman senator Caius Titus, but that origin is not attested.
today: Get it in writing. And the reason this channel has its name.
image: Johannes Vermeer - Girl Reading a Letter by an Open Window - Google Art Project.jpg
credit: Johannes Vermeer, Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window, c. 1657–59

translation: If you want to be loved, love.
origin: Seneca, Letters 9, quoting the Stoic philosopher Hecato: he promises a love potion without drugs or spells.
today: The only reliable recipe.
image: Lawrence Alma-Tadema - Ask Me No More.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, Ask Me No More, 1906

translation: A beard does not make a philosopher.
origin: A medieval proverb, echoing Plutarch and Aulus Gellius on men who looked like philosophers but were not.
today: Looking the part is not the same as knowing the job.
image: Caxton Aesop-010.jpg
commons_info: Avianus / Petrus Alphonsi / Poggio Bracciolini / Aesop / William Caxton / Joseph Jacobs |  | Public domain
credit: Woodcut from William Caxton's edition of Aesop's Fables, 1484

translation: The hood does not make the monk.
origin: A medieval proverb; Shakespeare quotes it in Twelfth Night.
today: Titles and uniforms prove nothing about the person wearing them.
image: Eduard von Grützner Mönch Zeichnung 1905.jpg
credit: Eduard von Grützner, Monk, 1905

translation: While I breathe, I hope.
origin: A motto of uncertain origin, echoing Cicero's letters to Atticus: while there is life, there is said to be hope. It is the motto of South Carolina.
today: As long as you are still in the game, it is not over.
image: Assistants and George Frederic Watts - Hope - Google Art Project.jpg
commons_info: George Frederic Watts and workshop | 1886date QS:P571,+1886-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: George Frederic Watts and assistants, Hope, 1886

translation: An excuse not asked for is an obvious accusation.
origin: A medieval legal maxim.
today: If you defend yourself before anyone accuses you, people will wonder why.
image: The Denial of Saint Peter-Caravaggio (1610).jpg
credit: Caravaggio, The Denial of Saint Peter, 1610

translation: Do not cast pearls before swine.
origin: The Vulgate, Matthew 7:6, from the Sermon on the Mount.
today: Do not waste good things on people who cannot appreciate them.
image: Pieter Brueghel II - The Netherlandish Proverbs 2018 CKS 15496 0007.jpg
commons_info: Pieter Brueghel the Younger | 1600 | Public domain
credit: Pieter Brueghel the Younger, Netherlandish Proverbs, 17th century

translation: First, do no harm.
origin: Not in the Hippocratic Oath. The idea is in the Hippocratic Epidemics; the Latin formula appears in the 19th century.
today: Before trying to fix something, make sure you are not making it worse.
image: David-Antiochus et Stratonice.jpg
credit: Jacques-Louis David, Erasistratus Discovering the Cause of Antiochus' Illness, 1774

translation: Rumour grows as it goes.
origin: Adapted from Virgil, Aeneid 4, where Rumour is a monster that gathers strength as it travels.
today: By the time a story reaches you, it has usually grown.
image: Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Dido and Aeneas - N00494 - National Gallery.jpg
commons_info: J. M. W. Turner | 1814 | Public domain
credit: J. M. W. Turner, Dido and Aeneas, 1814

translation: I believe because it is absurd.
origin: Misattributed to Tertullian. What he wrote, about the death of Christ, is that it is credible because it is foolish.
today: Now used for belief that ignores evidence, often unfairly to Tertullian.
image: Der ungläubige Thomas - Michelangelo Merisi, named Caravaggio.jpg
credit: Caravaggio, The Incredulity of Saint Thomas, c. 1601–02

translation: Disaster is virtue's opportunity.
origin: Seneca, On Providence 4.
today: Character shows in a crisis, not in calm weather.
image: Benjamin West (1738-1820) - The Departure of Regulus - RCIN 405416 - Royal Collection.jpg
credit: Benjamin West, The Departure of Regulus from Rome, 1769

translation: Who has begun has half done.
origin: Horace, Epistles 1.2, the line just before sapere aude.
today: Starting is the hardest part. Start.
image: Turner Dido Building Carthage.jpg
commons_info: J. M. W. Turner | 1815date QS:P571,+1815-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 | Public domain
credit: J. M. W. Turner, Dido Building Carthage, 1815

translation: What is badly gained is badly lost.
origin: A line of the early Roman poet Naevius, quoted by Cicero in the Second Philippic against Mark Antony.
today: Easy, dishonest money rarely stays.
image: Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema - The Meeting of Antony and Cleopatra.jpg
credit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, The Meeting of Antony and Cleopatra, 1885

latin: Quod licet Iovi, non licet bovi
pronunciation: kwod LI-ket YOH-wee, nohn LI-ket BOH-wee
translation: What is allowed to Jupiter is not allowed to the ox.
origin: A medieval proverb, recalling the myth of Jupiter turning into a bull.
today: Rules often differ for the powerful. Said with resignation or irritation.
image: Tizian 085.jpg
credit: Titian, The Rape of Europa, 1560–62

translation: Grasp the subject, the words will follow.
origin: Cato the Elder, in advice on public speaking preserved by a later writer on rhetoric.
today: Know your material and you will not need a script.
image: Demosthenes on the Seashore P379.jpg
credit: Eugène Delacroix, Demosthenes on the Seashore, 1859
